Standard deviations of position and momentum and lower bound.
Experimental Bell inequality violations and contributions of Clauser, Aspect and Zeilinger; interpret broad popular claims cautiously.
Development and experimental interpretation of Bell tests.
Wavefunction as complex amplitude, Born probability density and superposition.

historical_claims.anchor: In 1989, Akira Tonomura and colleagues reported a demonstration of the gradual buildup of an electron interference pattern using an electron microscope, an electron biprism and a position-sensitive counting system.
An electrostatic electron biprism provided two coherent alternatives that could interfere.
historical_claims.source_locator: Electron biprism, not literally two physical slits

historical_claims.anchor: In the standard theory, we represent the system with a quantum state.
The probability that it passes both filters is one quarter.
The uncertainty relation says that the product of the position standard deviation and the momentum standard deviation cannot be smaller than the reduced Planck constant divided by two.
In the nonrelativistic approximation, that corresponds to a velocity spread of at least about sixty thousand meters per second.
John Bell showed that broad classes of local hidden-variable accounts, subject to particular assumptions, obey bounds that quantum predictions can exceed.
Experiments by John Clauser, Alain Aspect, Anton Zeilinger and many later groups established such violations; their work was recognized by the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics.

description: Develops quantum states and probabilities using single-electron interference, distinguishing measured outcomes from the mathematical description of the experiment.
